paper_title: SoloQ: Calibration-Free Quantization for Diffusion Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Diffusion large language models dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive language models through bidirectional diffusion-based token generation. However, their growing model sizes and high inference costs make efficient deployment challenging: full-sequence denoising repeatedly invokes compute-intensive forward passes, while block-diffusion models additionally introduce a memory-intensive KV-cache. Low-bit weight-activation quantization is therefore attractive, yet existing dLLM post-training quantization methods rely on calibration data despite activation distributions shifting across masking states and denoising steps. We present SoloQ, a calibration-free quantization framework that maps weights and activations into a normalized rotated basis with a predictable marginal distribution, enabling data-independent quantization. SoloQ combines a structured K-RPBH rotation with a lightweight rescaling correction for calibration-free quantization. Its predictable post-rotation distribution supports both distribution-matched codebooks and hardware-native NVFP4. For block-diffusion models, SoloQ further applies commit-time KV-cache quantization to compress persistent states without perturbing the actively denoised block. Across full-sequence dLLMs (LLaDA and Dream) and block-diffusion dLLMs(Fast-dLLM v2 and Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion), SoloQ retains accuracy under 4-bit quantization and outperforms calibration-based baselines on knowledge- and reasoning-intensive benchmarks. With NVFP4, SoloQ reduces peak memory by up to 2.61X and accelerates end-to-end inference by up to 2.24X.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress across wide range of language understanding, reasoning, and generation tasks (Brown et al., 2020; Achiam et al., 2023; Touvron et al., 2023; Team et al., 2023), with autoregressive (AR) modeling remaining the dominant paradigm for text generation. In parallel, diffusion models (Bao et al., 2023; Peebles & Xie, 2023) have become powerful generative framework for continuous domains such as image and video generation (Esser et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025), where iterative denoising enables high-quality and flexible generation. Motivated by these advances, recent diffusion large language models (dLLMs) extend diffusion-based generation to discrete text, replacing strictly left-to-right decoding with iterative masked denoising and bidirectional context. Representative models such as LLaDA (Nie et al., 2026) and Dream (Ye et al., 2025) have demonstrated competitive language understanding, reasoning, and generation capabilities, suggesting that strong language modeling is not inherently tied to AR decoding. More recently, block-diffusion models (Wu et al., 2026a; Fu et al., 2026; Team et al., 2026) further bridge diffusion-based generation and practical inference by generating multiple tokens within block and reusing previously generated context through caching. Together, these developments establish diffusion-based language modeling as promising alternative to conventional AR generation. Despite this progress, efficient dLLM inference remains challenging as model size and context length grow. Unlike AR decoding, dLLMs iteratively refine multiple tokens in parallel across denoising steps, while long-context inference increases the memory and computation associated with activations and KV-cache. To better understand these bottlenecks, we profile Fast-dLLM v2 (Wu 1 Figure 1: Profiling and motivation for SOLOQ. (a) Memory breakdown at batch size 128 and aggregate linear/attention latency at batch size 1 for Fast-dLLM v2 (Wu et al., 2026a) across context lengths on an H200 GPU. (b) Layer-wise variation in down proj input activation scale across denoising steps, normalized to the first step. (c) Accuracy of PTQ (Ashkboos et al., 2024; Frantar et al., 2022) with WinoGrande/MMLU calibration versus calibration-free SOLOQ. et al., 2026a) from memory and latency perspectives, as shown in Figure 1(a). At short contexts, weights dominate the memory footprint, but the relative contribution of activations and the KV-cache grows with context length. In terms of latency, attention becomes expensive as the sequence length grows. In dLLMs, these costs are repeatedly incurred across denoising steps, making weight-only compression insufficient for efficient inference. Instead, low-bit quantization of weights, activations, and KV-cache can reduce both computation and memory across context regimes. Post-training quantization (PTQ) has been widely studied for AR LLMs to reduce memory and computation without retraining. Existing LLM PTQ methods span several complementary paradigms, including second-order methods that exploit Hessian information for low-bit weight quantization (Frantar et al., 2022; Li et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026b), scalingand salience-based methods that mitigate activation outliers through scaling or reparameterization (Xiao et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2024), and rotation-based methods that transform weights and activations into more quantization-friendly representations (Chee et al., 2023; Ashkboos et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025). These methods enable efficient low-bit inference while preserving accuracy. However, quantization on dLLMs is more challenging than AR LLMs. During diffusion decoding, the model repeatedly encounters different masking states and denoising steps, leading to substantial variation in activation distributions and quantization sensitivity throughout generation, as shown in Figure 1(b). Existing dLLM PTQ methods (Zhang et al., 2026; Xu & Yang, 2025; Yan et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026) rely on calibration data to capture or compensate for these stateand time-dependent variations. Figure 1(c) illustrates this sensitivity for representative calibrationbased PTQ method (Ashkboos et al., 2024; Frantar et al., 2022): changing calibration data from WinoGrande to MMLU alters accuracy across the benchmarks, showing that calibration choices may not generalize across tasks. This motivates different direction: rather than tracking changing distribution, can we transform it into predictable form that can be quantized without calibration? To realize this principle, we propose SOLOQ, calibration-free dLLM quantization framework that avoids calibration-set dependence while maintaining strong performance, as shown in Figure 1(c). Rather than adapting to activation distributions that vary across masking states and denoising steps, SOLOQ transforms weights and activations into normalized rotated space with predictable dimension-dependent marginal distribution. This enables data-independent quantization that can be shared across diffusion states without calibration. To support arbitrary transformer dimensions, SOLOQ introduces Kronecker-extended randomized permuted block-Hadamard (K-RPBH) rotation that combines efficient local mixing with global cross-block mixing. We further introduce scale-only bias correction that restores the radial component of low-bit quantized representations with negligible overhead. For block-diffusion models, SOLOQ extends the same calibration-free design to persistent KV states through commit-time KV-cache quantization. Built on these components, SOLOQ supports both distribution-matched codebook quantization and hardware-native NVFP4 without chasing activation distributions. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce SOLOQ, calibration-free dLLM quantization framework combining KRPBH rotation with lightweight scale-only bias correction. The resulting single predictable distribution supports both distribution-matched codebooks and hardware-native NVFP4 within the same calibration-free framework. 2 We extend SOLOQ to block-diffusion models through commit-time KV-cache quantization, covering weights, activations, and persistent KV states. Across full-sequence and block-diffusion dLLMs, SOLOQ achieves strong 4-bit accuracy with up to 2.61 reduction in peak memory and 2.24 faster end-to-end inference.

sections.title:
2 RELATED WORK
2.1 DIFFUSION LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
sections.content: Diffusion-based text generation has evolved from early discrete and masked diffusion models (Austin et al., 2021a; Li et al., 2022; He et al., 2023) to large-scale diffusion language models that perform iterative denoising with bidirectional context. Recent full-sequence models such as LLaDA (Nie et al., 2026), LLaDA-1.5 (Zhu et al., 2026), and Dream (Ye et al., 2025) demonstrate competitive language understanding, reasoning, and generation at billion-parameter scale. Beyond full-sequence diffusion, block-based and hybrid approaches improve decoding efficiency by generating multiple tokens per block and reusing previously generated context, including Block Diffusion (Arriola et al., 2025), Fast-dLLM (Wu et al., 2026b), Fast-dLLM v2 (Wu et al., 2026a), and LLaDA2.X (Bie et al., 2025; 2026). More recent systems further broaden this design space: Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion (Fu et al., 2026) unifies autoregressive, diffusion, and self-speculative decoding, Nemotron-TwoTower (Reda et al., 2026) separates autoregressive context modeling from diffusion denoising, and DiffusionGemma (Team et al., 2026) scales block-diffusion generation to 26B mixture-of-experts model. These developments highlight the rapid progress of diffusion-based language modeling toward scalable and practical text generation. 2.2 CALIBRATION-FREE AND DATA-INDEPENDENT QUANTIZATION complementary line of research avoids calibration altogether by deriving quantizers from analytically known or data-independent distributions. TurboQuant (Zandieh et al., 2026) randomly rotates input vectors to induce known coordinate distribution, enabling coordinate-wise optimal quantization. PolarQuant (Han et al., 2025) similarly exploits an analytically known distribution after random preconditioning and polar transformation for online vector and KV-cache quantization. OrbitQuant (Lee et al., 2026a) extends this principle to image and video diffusion transformers using randomized permuted block-Hadamard rotations for calibration-free weightactivation quantization. ConvRot (Huang et al., 2025) applies group-wise Hadamard rotations for W4A4 diffusiontransformer quantization, while DVD-Quant (Li et al., 2026) combines data-free grid refinement, rotation, and adaptive bit-width allocation for video diffusion transformers. SOLOQ builds on this distributional perspective for diffusion language models, extending calibration-free quantization to arbitrary transformer dimensions and persistent KV states in block-diffusion models. 2.3 POST-TRAINING QUANTIZATION FOR DLLMS Recent work has begun to develop PTQ methods specifically for diffusion language models. QuantdLLM (Zhang et al., 2026) introduces masked calibration simulation for timestep-dependent masking and targets extreme low-bit weight quantization. DLLMQuant (Xu & Yang, 2025) accounts for temporal and masking variations for weightactivation quantization, while STaR-Quant (Yan et al., 2026) addresses state-dependent activation disparity and temporal error accumulation. FAIRCalib (Huang et al., 2026) improves calibration by emphasizing fragile token-commitment states. Despite their designs, existing dLLM PTQ methods remain calibration-based and focus on fullsequence diffusion models. To our knowledge, SOLOQ is the first calibration-free framework to support KV-cache quantization for block-diffusion models while also covering full-sequence dLLMs.

In contrast, block-diffusion models (Bie et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026a) reuse the KVcache of previously committed blocks, causing the persistent cache to grow with context length. As shown in Figure 1(a), this growth creates significant memory bottleneck at long context lengths. SOLOQ quantizes the KV-cache only when block is committed, as illustrated in Figure 2(c). The active denoising block remains in full precision, avoiding repeated quantization across denoising steps. Keys use KIVI-style per-channel asymmetric quantization (Liu et al., 2024), while values follow the SOLOQ activation path with K-RPBH and either LloydMax or NVFP4 quantization. This commit-time design avoids repeatedly quantizing the KV states of the actively denoised block while compressing only persistent states. The overall algorithm of SOLOQ is shown in Appendix B.

sections.title: 5.4 MEMORY AND LATENCY EFFICIENCY
sections.content: We measure the end-to-end inference efficiency of SOLOQ using optimized GPU kernel implementations. SOLOQ-C uses 8-bit Tensor Core kernels on NVIDIA H200 GPUs, while SOLOQ-N uses native NVFP4 kernels on an NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000. As shown in Figure 4, SOLOQ-N achieves 2.312.61 reduction in peak memory across five dLLMs, primarily through 4-bit weight storage and, for block-diffusion models, KV-cache compression. It also achieves 1.942.24 end-to-end speedup over BF16 across the evaluated workloads. For Nemotron, whose EOS trajectory changes after quantization, we compare the same BF16-recorded sequence of 75 forward passes and obtain 2.05 speedup. We further implement SOLOQ on an FPGA, as detailed in Appendix E.

sections.title: C EVALUATION DETAILS
sections.content: We retain each models official evaluation stack rather than enforcing unified harness, since identically named benchmarks can differ in prompting, inference, and grading. Within each model, FP and quantized runs use identical prompts, few-shot settings, batch sizes, generation parameters, and graders. For full-sequence models, we evaluate TruthfulQA (Lin et al., 2022), ARCChallenge (Clark et al., 2018), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2021), PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020), C-Eval (Huang et al., 2023), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), and GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021). For block-diffusion models, Human-B/P and MBPP-B/P denote the Base and Plus variants of HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021b), evaluated using EvalPlus (Liu et al., 2023). We additionally evaluate GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021), IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023), MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020), and GPQA (Rein et al., 2023). C.1 LLADA-8B-BASE For LLaDA-8B-Base, we follow the official LM Evaluation Harness setup (Gao et al., 2024). TruthfulQA-MC2, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande use 128 Monte Carlo masking samples, while MMLU and C-EVAL use one. TruthfulQA uses CFG 2.0, ARCChallenge/HellaSwag/PIQA use CFG 0.5, and the remaining tasks use CFG 0. WinoGrande, MMLU, and C-EVAL are 5-shot; the other likelihood tasks are zero-shot. All likelihood tasks report plain accuracy. GSM8K follows the official 5-shot setup with generation length, diffusion steps, and block length of 1,024 and strict-match scoring. HumanEval is zero-shot with the same generation configuration and reports pass@1. 17 C.2 LLADA-1.5 LLaDA-1.5 is evaluated with its official OpenCompass stack (Contributors, 2023) for ARCChallenge, HellaSwag, MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval. ARC-Challenge uses zero-shot generation with length/steps/block size 512; HellaSwag and MMLU use generation length/steps/block size 3, with MMLU evaluated 5-shot. GSM8K uses four in-prompt demonstrations with 256/256/16, and HumanEval uses 512/512/32. All generation tasks use greedy decoding and low-confidence remasking. ARC-Challenge and HellaSwag use first-option accuracy, MMLU reports the macro-average across 57 subjects, GSM8K uses answer extraction, and HumanEval reports pass@1. For compatibility with prior quantization work, TruthfulQA-MC2, WinoGrande, PIQA, and C-EVAL are additionally evaluated using the LLaDA-8B likelihood protocol; these columns are supplementary and not part of the official LLaDA-1.5 generation suite. C.3 DREAM-V0-BASE-7B including the Monte Carlo ELBO Dream-v0-Base-7B is evaluated with its native evaluator, likelihood tasks use 128 Monte estimator, autoregressive logit shift, and BOS token. All Carlo samples. ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, and TruthfulQA-MC2 are zero-shot, while WinoGrande, MMLU, and C-EVAL are 5-shot. We use batch size 32 for ARCChallenge/HellaSwag/PIQA/WinoGrande/TruthfulQA, 16 for MMLU, and 1 for C-EVAL; the reduced MMLU batch size is applied consistently to FP and quantized runs. ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, and PIQA report normalized accuracy, while the remaining likelihood tasks report accuracy. GSM8K uses 8-shot CoT prompting with 256 generated tokens and 256 diffusion steps; HumanEval is zero-shot with 512 generated tokens and 512 diffusion steps. TruthfulQA and C-EVAL are used only for controlled FP-to-quantized comparisons. C.4 FAST-DLLM V2 For Fast-dLLM v2, evaluation follows the official NVLabs adapter. GSM8K, Minerva MATH, and IFEval are zero-shot with batch size 32; MMLU is zero-shot and GPQA Main 5-shot with batch size 1. Generation uses block size 32, sub-block size 8, threshold 1, greedy decoding, and up to 2,048 new tokens. MMLU and GPQA are evaluated by likelihood rather than generation. GSM8K uses flexible answer extraction, Minerva MATH uses symbolic-equivalence rescoring, and IFEval reports prompt-level strict accuracy. HumanEval and MBPP use EvalPlus with batch size 32, reporting both base and Plus pass@1 after code sanitization. C.5 NEMOTRON-LABS-DIFFUSION-8B Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-8B is evaluated with the official inference implementation and NeMoSkills stack. All tasks, including MMLU and GPQA, are evaluated through generation with block length 32, threshold 0.9, temperature 0, batch size 1, and up to 8,192 generated tokens. Thinking mode and EOS early stopping are disabled. Since the Nemotron paper does not specify block length or EOS policy for its main table, we treat this as controlled operating point rather than an exact reconstruction. For the cross-model table, we evaluate GSM8K, Hendrycks MATH, IFEval, MMLU, GPQA Main, HumanEval, and MBPP. Mathematical tasks use the NeMo-Skills answer evaluator, MMLU and GPQA use generation-based multiple-choice scoring, HumanEval and MBPP use EvalPlus, and IFEval is averaged over its four strict/loose instruction-following metrics. MATH-500 and GPQA Diamond are reported only in comparisons matching the Nemotron papers benchmark configuration.

D.4 ATTENTION SINK IN DLLM Attention sinks, where small number of token positions receive disproportionately large attention mass, have also been observed in diffusion language models (Rulli et al., 2026). Figure 6 shows that this behavior persists in block-diffusion models: Fast-dLLM v2 exhibits pronounced sink at position 2, while Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion concentrates attention at position 0. Because such positions can play disproportionate role in attention computation, aggressively quantizing their KV states may cause larger degradation than quantizing ordinary positions. Table 11 shows that preserving the attention-sink position in full precision has little effect under W4A4KV4, suggesting that 4-bit KV quantization is sufficiently robust to the concentrated attention mass. In contrast, under the more aggressive W4A4KV2 setting, preserving the sink becomes beneficial. This indicates that sink-aware protection is mainly important at ultra-low KV precision, while standard 4-bit KV quantization can generally quantize the sink together with the remaining cache without noticeable degradation. We implement systolic-array accelerator with custom BF16 and NVFP4 datapaths on Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU104 FPGA and evaluate LLaDA-Base-8B for edge dLLM inference. Fig. 7(a) shows the hardware setup. The Zynq MPSoC consists of processing system (PS) and programmable logic 22 (PL), each with access to external DDR4 memory. The model weights are distributed across the PS and PL DDR4 memories, while activations are stored in the PL DDR4. As shown in Fig. 7(b), the systolic-array accelerator is implemented in the PL and receives execution instructions and portion of the model weights from the PS. The systolic array comprises multiply-and-accumulate (MAC) units together with input (IP), weight (W), and output (OP) buffers to perform tiled matrix multiplication on data tiles fetched from the PL DDR4. Fig. 7(c) summarizes the design specifications of the hardware accelerator. For the NVFP4 accelerator, we double the compute capacity because NVFP4 enables higher compute density than BF16. Fig. 8 shows the power breakdown of the accelerators during LLaDA-Base-8B inference, where the compute logic, DDR memories, PS processor, and clock generation and routing are the major contributors. The NVFP4 accelerator consumes 15% less power while providing twice the compute throughput of the BF16 design. As shown in Table 12, SOLOQs NVFP4 accelerator achieves 1.94 end-to-end speedup and 2.70 higher energy efficiency than BF16 on LLaDA-Base-8B.

sections.content: SOLOQ introduces online activation rotation to transform representations into the K-RPBH basis. Although weight rotations are performed offline, activation-side rotations incur additional inference overhead. Folding these rotations into adjacent weights can reduce this cost, but, as shown in Appendix D.3, the folded topology may degrade accuracy under low-bit quantization, particularly for block-diffusion models. In addition, SOLOQ-C uses non-uniform codebooks whose centroids are represented losslessly in INT8 for efficient computation. Consequently, its low-bit representation cannot directly exploit native 4-bit Tensor Core execution and instead relies on 8-bit kernels, resulting in lower speedups than the hardware-native NVFP4 path of SOLOQ-N. Finally, the full latency benefit of SOLOQ-N depends on hardware support for native NVFP4 computation; on devices without such support, its practical acceleration may be reduced.
